splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on when actuarial assumptions used to calculate employer withdrawal liability from multiemployer pension plans must be finalized. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers participating in multiemployer plans, as the timing directly controls how much withdrawing employers must pay.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability must be selected by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers greater predictability.

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that a plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing use of more current data.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts can apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. The outcome affects sentencing calculations at revocation hearings for thousands of individuals who abscond each year and raises questions about judicial power to extend punishment without explicit statutory authorization.

positions.label: Supervised release is tolled during absconding
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled when the supervisee absconds, extending the period during which violations can be found.

positions.label: Supervised release is not tolled
positions.summary: Holds that without explicit statutory authorization, courts may not toll the supervised release term when a supervisee absconds.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face a stricter gatekeeping requirement than Congress intended when bringing successive collateral attacks. If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners are categorically barred from raising any previously presented claim, in addition to Section 2255(h)'s requirements. If not, they need only satisfy 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new constitutional rule.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the categorical bar on relitigating previously raised claims in § 2244(b)(1) applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, imposing an additional gatekeeping hurdle.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s bar does not apply to federal prisoners' § 2255 motions, so they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s separate requirements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether and under what circumstances candidates can establish Article III standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures. The resolution affects how easily election rules on mail-in voting, ballot counting deadlines, and other election administration practices can be challenged before elections take place.

positions.label: Candidates have standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates have Article III standing to challenge election rules that allegedly dilute or affect the counting of their votes, even before the election occurs.

positions.label: Candidates lack standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates' alleged injuries from election rules like extended ballot-receipt deadlines are too speculative to confer Article III standing pre-election.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency or Sentencing Commission deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous provisions that affect criminal sentences.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts should defer to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations of ambiguous guidelines or regulatory provisions that increase criminal liability or sentences, or whether the rule of lenity should resolve the ambiguity in the defendant's favor. The Third Circuit has held that deference trumps lenity, while the Fourth, Fifth, and Eleventh Circuits hold that lenity prevails.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes precedence over Auer/Kisor deference when interpreting ambiguous provisions that affect criminal liability or sentencing, resolving ambiguity in the defendant's favor.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that courts should defer to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations of ambiguous guidelines provisions even in criminal sentencing contexts, rather than applying the rule of lenity.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether USSG § 4B1.2(b)'s definition of 'controlled substance offense' includes inchoate offenses like conspiracy, attempt, and aiding and abetting based on Application Note 1, or whether the guideline text unambiguously excludes such offenses.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether Sentencing Guidelines commentary (Application Note 1) can expand the definition of 'controlled substance offense' in § 4B1.2(b) to include inchoate offenses not mentioned in the guideline text. Some circuits defer to the commentary under Stinson, while others hold the text is unambiguous and excludes inchoate offenses. This split affects career-offender designations and dramatically changes sentencing ranges.

positions.label: Commentary validly includes inchoate offenses
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation of § 4B1.2(b) entitled to deference, and therefore conspiracy and other inchoate offenses qualify as controlled substance offenses for career-offender purposes.

positions.label: Guideline text excludes inchoate offenses
positions.summary: Holds that the text of § 4B1.2(b) is unambiguous in not including inchoate offenses, and Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the guideline's scope beyond its text.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether 'and' in § 3553(f)(1) means a defendant must meet all three listed criminal-history criteria to be disqualified from safety-valve relief, or whether possessing any one criterion is disqualifying. This determines whether district courts must impose sentences without regard to statutory minimums and creates sentencing disparities based on geography.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required to disqualify
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' conjunctively.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state schedule covers substances not listed on the federal Controlled Substances Act schedules.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' in § 4B1.2(b) requires the substance underlying a state conviction to also be federally controlled, or whether any state-controlled substance qualifies. This affects career-offender and other sentencing enhancements for defendants with prior state drug convictions.

positions.label: State schedule controls — no federal match required
positions.summary: Holds that an offense under state law qualifies as a controlled substance offense under the Guidelines regardless of whether the particular substance is controlled under federal law, because there is no textual basis to graft a federal limitation onto the guideline.

positions.label: Federal schedule controls — substance must be federally controlled
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction qualifies as a controlled substance offense only if the substance is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether non-retroactive changes in sentencing law can serve as extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release, either alone or combined with other factors. The Seventh and Eighth Circuits hold such changes cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons, while other circuits allow consideration of non-retroactive changes. The Sentencing Commission's 2024 policy statement amendment (§ 1B1.13(b)(6)) attempted to resolve the issue but its authority to do so is itself disputed.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law, whether offered alone or combined with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law may be considered as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release, particularly in combination with other factors.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may expressly punish a defendant for the underlying violation of supervised release conditions, as opposed to sanctioning only the breach of the court's trust.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts revoking supervised release may impose sentences as punishment for the violation conduct itself, or only to sanction the breach of trust inherent in violating the conditions. The Sixth Circuit allows express punishment for the violation, placing it at the extreme of a circuit split, while most other circuits hold revocation sentences should reflect only the seriousness of the breach of trust.

positions.label: May punish for underlying violation conduct
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for the conduct underlying the supervised release violation, not just for breaching the court's trust.

positions.label: May only sanction breach of trust
positions.summary: Holds that revocation of supervised release is primarily a sanction for the breach of the court's trust, and courts should not impose sentences as additional punishment for the underlying violation conduct.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners must bring challenges to conditions of confinement (as opposed to fact or duration of confinement) through habeas corpus under 28 U.S.C. § 2241, or whether they may also use civil rights actions such as Bivens.
splits.description: Circuits have long disagreed on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for all challenges by prisoners that touch on their confinement, or whether claims about conditions of confinement can be brought as civil rights actions. This split affects how federal prisoners challenge BOP decisions such as denial of early release credits under the First Step Act.

positions.label: Habeas is exclusive for conditions affecting duration
positions.summary: Holds that when a prisoner's challenge to conditions of confinement effectively seeks speedier release or affects the duration of confinement, habeas is the exclusive remedy.

positions.label: Conditions claims may proceed outside habeas
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to conditions of confinement, even those that may incidentally affect release timing, are not limited to habeas and may be brought through civil rights actions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the civil or criminal appeal deadline applies to appeals from orders on Hyde Amendment motions for attorney's fees in criminal cases.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter (subject to a 30-day appeal deadline) or a criminal matter (subject to a 14-day appeal deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies because the motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, but acknowledged a lopsided circuit split.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that Hyde Amendment motions for attorney's fees are civil matters ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that Hyde Amendment motions arise within and are part of the criminal case, so the shorter 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) applies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's property belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 348(f)(1)(A)'s reference to 'property of the estate, as of the date of filing of the petition' means that post-petition appreciation in asset value belongs to the estate or the debtor upon conversion. This affects whether Chapter 7 trustees can sell assets to recover appreciation that occurred during the Chapter 13 case.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion increases in property equity belong to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7, based on the broad scope of § 541(a).

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation in property value belongs to the debtor, consistent with § 348(f)'s purpose of protecting good-faith converting debtors.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve questions about legal standards for business establishment discrimination claims, indicating the Second Circuit's approach was sufficiently unsettled or in conflict with other circuits to warrant review. The decision could impact hospitality, retail, and other service industries nationwide.

positions.label: Second Circuit approach
positions.summary: The Second Circuit applied standards for discrimination or unfair treatment claims in hospitality that SCOTUS found warranted review, suggesting a potential conflict with other circuits.

positions.label: Alternative approach
positions.summary: Other circuits may apply different standards for evaluating discrimination claims in business establishments, creating the conflict that prompted SCOTUS review.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: Circuits have taken different approaches to whether denials of motions to seal medical records are immediately appealable as collateral orders under 28 U.S.C. § 1291. The D.C. Circuit held that maintaining privacy in medical treatments and diagnoses is a value of 'high order' warranting immediate appellate review, but this approach may conflict with other circuits' narrower application of the collateral order doctrine.

positions.label: Immediately appealable under collateral order doctrine
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal medical records are immediately appealable because medical privacy is a value of high order that would be effectively unreviewable after final judgment.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that denials of motions to seal are interlocutory orders not subject to immediate appeal, as the privacy interest can be adequately vindicated through other means or on appeal from final judgment.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state law categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violates the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated sex-based biological advantages, and whether as-applied equal protection challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether categorical bans on transgender athlete participation survive intermediate scrutiny when applied to individuals who have undergone medical transition. The case also raises the broader question of whether sex-based classifications affecting transgender individuals warrant heightened scrutiny.

positions.label: Categorical ban violates Equal Protection as applied
positions.summary: Holds that a categorical ban fails intermediate scrutiny as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated biological advantages, because the state has not shown the ban is substantially related to its interest in competitive fairness for this subclass.

positions.label: Categorical ban does not violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that biological sex-based classifications in athletics are substantially related to the important governmental interest in fair competition and the safety of female athletes, even as applied to transgender women.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
